To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) stable isotopes in teeth of Toxodon indicate that it was a mixed-feeding notoungulate, with preference for C4 plants; (2) stable isotopes indicate that Stegomastodon fed mainly on C3 plants, although with less C4 in the diet compared with African elephants; (3) δ 18 O values in both taxa seem more related to the isotopic composition in the ingested water than to the plants of which these mammals fed.

the isotopic values of δ 13 C of the extinct notoungulate and proboscidean mammals from southern Brazil indicate that they were mixed-feeders, with preference for C4 plants, and that their δ 18 O values seem to reflect the water isotopic composition rather than the isotopes in the plants they consumed.

Toxodon and Stgomastodon were mixed feeders, with Toxodon feeding mostly on C4 grasses and Stgomastodont on a more C3 diet; and the δ 18 O isotopic values in these taxa are more influenced by the isotopic composition in the ingested water than in the plants of their diets.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the isotopic signatures of the analyzed fossils are compatible with the paleoenvironments and paleoclimatic conditions reconstructed from other lines of evidence, including fossil pollen and paleosols.
stable isotope analyses of fossil mammalian teeth can be a powerful tool to reconstruct paleoenvironmental conditions in South American Pleistocene localities.
